children.title: Scaled Residual Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Meaning of residual quantities after solver or problem scaling.

assumptions_latex: The original split constraint is \(Ax-z=0\).
The scalings \(D\) and \(E\) are nonsingular positive diagonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaled residuals are weighted coordinates of the original residuals and must be interpreted through the inverse scaling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact diagonal coordinate correspondence for primal and stationarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(x=D\bar x\), \(\bar z=Ez\), \(\bar A=EAD\), \(\bar P=D^{\mathsf T}PD\), \(\bar q=D^{\mathsf T}q\), and \(\bar y=E^{-\mathsf T}y\). For \(r_p=Ax-z\) and \(r_d=Px+q+A^{\mathsf T}y\), the residuals of the scaled formulation satisfy \[\bar r_p=\bar A\bar x-\bar z=Er_p,\qquad \bar r_d=\bar P\bar x+\bar q+\bar A^{\mathsf T}\bar y=D^{\mathsf T}r_d.\] Therefore a scaled residual is not an invariant physical error: the corresponding unscaled residuals are \(r_p=E^{-1}\bar r_p\) and \(r_d=D^{-\mathsf T}\bar r_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under diagonal row and variable scaling, primal and stationarity residuals are multiplied by E and D-transpose; inverse scaling recovers their original interpretation.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Residual Interpretation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal coordinate transformations and inverse interpretations are internally consistent and fit a representation leaf, but the record has no inspectable source for this exact residual-scaling correspondence.

children.title: Unscaled Residual Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Meaning of residual quantities in the original QP units.

knowledge_statements.title: Unscaled Residual Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original-coordinate KKT residuals for a convex QP with a split constraint variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x \tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x\) subject to \(Ax=z\) and \(z\in C\), where \(P\succeq0\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is closed and convex. For an iterate \((x,z,y)\), the unscaled primal and dual residuals are \[r_{\mathrm p}=Ax-z,\qquad r_{\mathrm d}=Px+q+A^\top y.\] Thus \(r_{\mathrm p}\) measures violation of the splitting equality in the original constraint units, while \(r_{\mathrm d}\) measures violation of stationarity in the original objective-gradient units. If additionally \(z\in C\) and \(y\in N_C(z)\), then \(r_{\mathrm p}=0\) and \(r_{\mathrm d}=0\) are exactly the KKT feasibility and stationarity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unscaled primal and dual residuals measure equality-feasibility and stationarity errors in the original problem coordinates and physical units.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(q\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\((x,z,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times C\times\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm p}=Ax-z\) and \(r_{\mathrm d}=Px+q+A^\top y\) are the original-coordinate KKT residuals.

notation.meaning: normal cone of C at z

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct residual form of the split convex-QP KKT system
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate to the leaf, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Residual Rescaling Correspondence
children.top_down_role: How scaled residual evidence maps back to original problem coordinates and units.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Rescaling Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence under invertible diagonal variable, constraint, and objective scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(E\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be invertible diagonal matrices and let \(\alpha>0\). Set \(x=D\bar x\), \(\bar z=Ez\), and \(\bar y=\alpha E^{-\top}y\), with \(\bar P=\alpha D^\top PD\), \(\bar q=\alpha D^\top q\), and \(\bar A=EAD\). If \(r_{\mathrm p}=Ax-z\) and \(r_{\mathrm d}=Px+q+A^\top y\), then the scaled residuals satisfy \[\bar r_{\mathrm p}=\bar A\bar x-\bar z=Er_{\mathrm p},\qquad \bar r_{\mathrm d}=\bar P\bar x+\bar q+\bar A^\top\bar y=\alpha D^\top r_{\mathrm d}.\] Consequently, \(r_{\mathrm p}=E^{-1}\bar r_{\mathrm p}\) and \(r_{\mathrm d}=\alpha^{-1}D^{-\top}\bar r_{\mathrm d}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled and original residuals correspond through invertible linear maps, so either representation can be recovered exactly from the other.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(E\) are invertible diagonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar r_{\mathrm p}=Er_{\mathrm p}\) and \(\bar r_{\mathrm d}=\alpha D^\top r_{\mathrm d}\), with the displayed inverse transformations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identities follow from the stated invertible coordinate transformation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rescaling identities follow consistently from the stated transformations and fit the leaf, but no source or specific locator supports the convention.

children.title: Residual Balance as a Tuning Signal

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Balance as a Tuning Signal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heuristic penalty adaptation using comparable normalized primal and dual residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat r_{\mathrm p}\ge0\) and \(\widehat r_{\mathrm d}\ge0\) be dimensionless, comparably normalized primal and dual residual norms for a splitting method with penalty \(\rho>0\). For constants \(\mu>1\) and \(\tau>1\), a residual-balancing policy may set \[\rho^+=\begin{cases}\tau\rho,&\widehat r_{\mathrm p}>\mu\widehat r_{\mathrm d},\\ \rho/\tau,&\widehat r_{\mathrm d}>\mu\widehat r_{\mathrm p},\\ \rho,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] Increasing \(\rho\) emphasizes primal agreement, while decreasing it emphasizes dual progress. This rule is a tuning signal rather than an optimality certificate; convergence guarantees require the underlying method's conditions for variable penalties, including any required dual-variable rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large normalized primal-to-dual residual ratio suggests increasing the splitting penalty; the opposite imbalance suggests decreasing it.
assumptions_latex: The two residual measures are dimensionless and comparably normalized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual imbalance determines the displayed heuristic update of \(\rho\), but does not itself certify QP optimality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard residual-balancing heuristic for operator-splitting methods
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and heuristic qualification are appropriate, but the update convention, its interpretation, and required dual rescaling are method-dependent and unsupported by a cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-separation certificate for infeasibility of affine membership constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constraint system \(Ax\in C\), where \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, define its support function by \(\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{z\in C}y^\top z\). A vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \[A^\top y=0,\qquad \sigma_C(y)<0\] is a primal-infeasibility certificate. Indeed, every hypothetical feasible \(x\) would give \(y^\top Ax=0\), whereas \(Ax\in C\) implies \(y^\top Ax\le\sigma_C(y)<0\). For \(C=[l,u]\), the support value is \(u^\top y_+ +l^\top y_-\), interpreted componentwise in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier annihilating the range of A while strictly separating that range from the constraint set certifies primal infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\sigma_C(y)\) is finite at the proposed certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A^\top y=0\) and \(\sigma_C(y)<0\), then no \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Ax\in C\).

notation.meaning: componentwise positive and negative parts of y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional strong-separation certificate for affine convex feasibility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed conditions give a valid sufficient separation certificate and the certificate content kind fits the leaf, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Dual Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificate semantics for failure of dual feasibility or dual solvability.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction certificate showing unbounded descent of a feasible convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x \tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x\) subject to \(Ax\in C\), with \(P\succeq0\). A nonzero vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \[Pd=0,\qquad Ad\in C^\infty,\qquad q^\top d<0\] is a dual-infeasibility certificate, provided the primal feasible set is nonempty. For every feasible \(x_0\), the ray \(x_0+td\) remains feasible for \(t\ge0\), and its objective equals \(f(x_0)+tq^\top d\); hence it tends to \(-\infty\). The terminology reflects the consequent absence of a finite primal-dual KKT solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A null-curvature feasible recession direction with negative linear cost proves that the primal objective is unbounded below and no dual optimum exists.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
There exists \(x_0\) with \(Ax_0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditions imply \(\inf\{\tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x:Ax\in C\}=-\infty\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated feasibility assumption, the conditions correctly imply unbounded descent. A source is required for both the recession criterion and the solver-specific term “dual infeasibility certificate.”

children.title: Primal Recession Certificates
children.top_down_role: Feasible recession evidence associated with absence of a finite primal optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Recession Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable direction generating a feasible ray with nonincreasing quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex QP feasible set \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\in C\}\), a vector \(d\ne0\) with \(Ad\in C^\infty\) is a primal recession certificate: for every \(x\in F\) and \(t\ge0\), \(x+td\in F\). If additionally \(Pd=0\), then along this ray \[f(x+td)=f(x)+tq^\top d.\] Hence \(q^\top d<0\) certifies unbounded descent, while \(q^\top d=0\) certifies a flat feasible recession direction. Without \(Pd=0\), positive quadratic curvature can prevent objective recession even though feasibility recedes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction mapped into the constraint set's recession cone preserves feasibility; null quadratic curvature determines whether it also yields objective recession.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ad\in C^\infty\) gives a feasible ray, and \(Pd=0\) reduces its objective change to \(tq^\top d\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recession-cone characterization of affine convex constraints
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-recession and null-curvature statements are correct for the stated convex QP and fit a certificate leaf, but they lack cited evidence.

children.title: Dual-Infeasibility Recession Correspondence
children.top_down_role: QP-specific relationship between dual infeasibility evidence and primal recession directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Infeasibility Recession Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between descending feasible rays and recession of the constraint set restricted to the range of the affine map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and suppose \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\in C\}\ne\varnothing\). Define \(R=C\cap\operatorname{range}(A)\) and \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x\). For any \(d\ne0\), the conditions \[Pd=0,\qquad Ad\in R^\infty,\qquad q^\top d<0\] hold if and only if, for every \(x_0\in F\), the ray \(x_0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\) and satisfies \[f(x_0+td)=f(x_0)+tq^\top d\longrightarrow-\infty.\] In particular, the conventional sufficient certificate condition \(Ad\in C^\infty\), together with \(Pd=0\) and \(q^\top d<0\), implies this descending-ray property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Descending zero-curvature feasible rays correspond exactly to recession directions of the constraint set restricted to the range of A; membership in the recession cone of all C is a sufficient conventional certificate condition.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\in C\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditions \(Pd=0\), \(Ad\in R^\infty\), and \(q^\top d<0\) are equivalent to the stated feasible descending-ray property.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Infeasibility Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate-Difference Certificate Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction and testing of candidate recession directions from consecutive splitting iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given consecutive iterates \((x^{k-1},y^{k-1})\) and \((x^k,y^k)\), form \(\Delta x^k=x^k-x^{k-1}\) and \(\Delta y^k=y^k-y^{k-1}\). If \(\Delta y^k\ne0\), set \(v^k=\Delta y^k/\|\Delta y^k\|_\infty\) and test the approximate primal-infeasibility conditions for \(v^k\). children.title: Absolute Tolerance Policies

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Tolerance Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-independent termination using fixed residual thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_{\mathrm p}^k\) and \(r_{\mathrm d}^k\) be unscaled primal and dual residuals at iteration \(k\), and choose absolute tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}^{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm d}^{\mathrm{abs}}\ge0\). An absolute-tolerance termination policy declares approximate KKT satisfaction exactly when \[\|r_{\mathrm p}^k\|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}^{\mathrm{abs}},\qquad \|r_{\mathrm d}^k\|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm d}^{\mathrm{abs}},\] together with any separately required membership or complementarity tests. The residual norm and coordinate system must be fixed in advance. Because the thresholds do not scale with problem data or iterate magnitude, rescaling the QP can change whether the same physical iterate passes.

children.title: Relative Tolerance Policies
children.top_down_role: Stopping policies normalized by problem, iterate, or data magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Tolerance Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-dependent termination relative to reference magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_{\mathrm p}^k\) and \(r_{\mathrm d}^k\) be primal and dual residuals, and let \(s_{\mathrm p}^k,s_{\mathrm d}^k\ge0\) be nonnegative reference scales formed from corresponding KKT terms. For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}^{\mathrm{rel}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm d}^{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\), a purely relative policy accepts iteration \(k\) when \[\lVert r_{\mathrm p}^k\rVert\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}^{\mathrm{rel}}s_{\mathrm p}^k,\qquad \lVert r_{\mathrm d}^k\rVert\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm d}^{\mathrm{rel}}s_{\mathrm d}^k.\] Typical scales are maxima of norms of the terms whose difference or sum forms each residual. If a reference scale vanishes, this policy requires the corresponding residual to vanish; practical solvers therefore commonly add an absolute tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative stopping compares each residual norm with a relative tolerance times a matching KKT reference scale, and requires a zero residual when that scale is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(s_{\mathrm p}^k,s_{\mathrm d}^k\ge0\) use the same coordinates and norm as their residuals.

children.title: Mixed-Tolerance Scaling Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Tolerance Scaling Regimes

Under diagonal problem scaling, the residuals, reference scales, and absolute tolerances must be transformed consistently before the scaled- and unscaled-coordinate tests can be considered equivalent.

children.title: Duality-Gap Thresholds

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed absolute-relative gap test for convex QPs with available feasible primal and dual objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_k\) and \(d_k\) be finite primal and dual objective values obtained from primal- and dual-feasible iterates, so weak duality gives \(g_k:=p_k-d_k\ge 0\). Given \(\varepsilon_g^{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_g^{\mathrm{rel}}\ge 0\), define \(s_k:=\max\{1,|p_k|,|d_k|\}\). The duality-gap threshold is satisfied exactly when \[g_k\le \varepsilon_g^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_g^{\mathrm{rel}}s_k.\] If either iterate is infeasible, this test alone is not an optimality certificate and must be combined with feasibility and stationarity tests.

children.title: Joint Termination Logic
children.top_down_role: Policies coordinating gap tests with residual tests under conjunctive or prioritized acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Termination Logic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjunctive optimality termination using gap, feasibility, and stationarity tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an iterate and associated residuals at iteration \(k\), first evaluate the gap predicate \(G_k\), primal-residual predicate \(P_k\), and dual-residual predicate \(D_k\) using their declared mixed tolerances. Set \(T_k:=G_k\land P_k\land D_k\). If \(T_k\) is true, terminate and return the iterate with status \(\mathrm{SOLVED}\) and the three measured quantities. Otherwise continue unless an independent budget or interruption rule applies. Thus no small gap can compensate for a failed residual test, and no small residual can compensate for a failed valid-gap test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declare a QP solved only when its gap, primal residual, and dual residual tests all pass; otherwise continue or apply a separate budget rule.
assumptions_latex: Each predicate is evaluated using the same iterate index \(k\).
The gap predicate is used only when its primal-dual values are valid.
No overriding failure status has already occurred.

knowledge_statements.title: Application-Accuracy Termination

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\) be the current QP iterate, let \(x^\star\) be an exact solution, and let \(L_{\mathrm{app}}(x_k,x^\star)\ge0\) measure downstream application error. Suppose a computable estimator \(E_k\) satisfies \(L_{\mathrm{app}}(x_k,x^\star)\le E_k\) for every admissible exact solution. Given application tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm{app}}\ge0\), application-accuracy termination is permitted when \[E_k\le\tau_{\mathrm{app}}.\] The returned record must identify the estimator and assumptions supporting its upper-bound property.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Budget Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard elapsed-time stopping rule independent of mathematical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t_0\) be the monotonic-clock time immediately before solver work begins, let \(t_k\) be the time at the latest interruptible checkpoint, and let \(T_{\max}>0\) be the permitted elapsed-time budget. Define \(e_k:=t_k-t_0\). Wall-clock termination is triggered at the first checkpoint satisfying \[e_k\ge T_{\max}.\] The solver returns its best retained iterate and measured certificates, but budget exhaustion alone does not assign an optimality or infeasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the first checkpoint where elapsed monotonic time reaches the budget, return the best retained iterate without claiming convergence.

The algorithm exposes interruptible checkpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Exhaustion Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-readable status representation distinguishing resource exhaustion from mathematical solution claims.

A valid record reports termination by resource exhaustion only and makes no claim of optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Residual Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A small absolute stationarity residual need not imply accurate decision variables without a uniform residual-to-solution error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), consider the unconstrained QP \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}} f_\mu(x):=\frac{\mu}{2}(x-1)^2.\] Its unique solution is \(x^\star=1\). At \(x_0=0\), the stationarity residual is \(|\nabla f_\mu(x_0)|=\mu\), while \(|x_0-x^\star|=1\). Hence, for every fixed absolute residual tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(0<\mu\le\varepsilon\) causes the residual-only rule \(|\nabla f_\mu(x)|\le\varepsilon\) to accept \(x_0\), although its decision error remains one. Therefore an absolute stationarity-residual threshold alone gives no uniform decision-variable accuracy guarantee over this QP family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small curvature makes the gradient residual pass a fixed absolute tolerance at a point that remains one unit from the optimizer, so the residual threshold alone gives no uniform variable-accuracy guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The stopping rule uses only \(|\nabla f_\mu(x)|\le\varepsilon\).
The QP family permits arbitrarily small \(\mu>0\).
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\mu\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow |\nabla f_\mu(0)|\le\varepsilon\) while \(|0-x^\star|=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Distorted Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent constraint scaling can arbitrarily change an absolute feasibility residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), consider the equivalent equality-constrained QPs \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\frac12x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad \alpha x=\alpha.\] Every member has the unique feasible point \(x^\star=1\). At \(x_0=0\), the raw equality residual equals \(|\alpha x_0-\alpha|=\alpha\), although the distance to feasibility is \(|x_0-x^\star|=1\). For any absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(0<\alpha\le\varepsilon\) makes the raw residual pass. Thus an unscaled certificate is not invariant under equivalent row scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying an equality by a small positive number makes its raw residual arbitrarily small without changing either the feasible set or distance to feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The feasibility test uses the raw residual \(|\alpha x-\alpha|\le\varepsilon\).
No row normalization or relative scaling is applied.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\alpha\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow |\alpha x_0-\alpha|\le\varepsilon\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x_0,\{1\})=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Infeasibility Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite feasibility tolerances cannot distinguish certain inconsistent systems from nearby feasible perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta>0\), consider the inconsistent constraints \(x=0\) and \(x=\delta\) on \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). At \(\bar x=\delta/2\), both absolute residuals equal \(\delta/2\). Consequently, any feasibility rule accepting both residuals when they do not exceed \(\varepsilon\) declares approximate feasibility whenever \(0<\delta\le2\varepsilon\), despite exact infeasibility. The same observations are consistent with feasible systems obtained by perturbing either right-hand side by \(\delta\). Thus residuals at finite precision alone cannot resolve infeasibility below the data-uncertainty scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two contradictory equalities can have simultaneously tiny residuals, making exact infeasibility indistinguishable from a nearby feasible perturbation at finite tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is judged by separate absolute residual bounds of \(\varepsilon>0\).
Right-hand-side uncertainty is at least of order \(\delta\).
No exact-arithmetic infeasibility certificate is available.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean projection access model for a nonempty closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A Euclidean projection oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_C\) that, for every query \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), returns the unique point \[\mathcal{O}_C(z)=\Pi_C(z):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2.\] In the projection-oracle access model, an algorithm may submit adaptive queries and receives only the projected points; one oracle call is charged per projection. Exact uniqueness follows from closed convexity and the strict convexity of the squared Euclidean distance.

children.title: Coupled Oracle Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Oracle Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work accounting for iterations coupling one gradient evaluation with one feasible-set projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) on a closed convex set \(C\). Suppose each iteration evaluates \(Qx+c\) once and computes \(P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\|u-z\|_2\) once. If their respective costs are \(C_{\mathrm{grad}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{proj}}\), while scalar-vector work costs \(C_{\mathrm{aux}}\), then \(k\) iterations have oracle work \[W_k=k\bigl(C_{\mathrm{grad}}+C_{\mathrm{proj}}+C_{\mathrm{aux}}\bigr).\] Hence an iteration bound \(k\le N(\varepsilon)\) yields \(W(\varepsilon)\le N(\varepsilon)(C_{\mathrm{grad}}+C_{\mathrm{proj}}+C_{\mathrm{aux}})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every iteration uses one gradient and one projection, total work is the iteration count times their combined cost, including auxiliary vector operations.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Oracle costs are measured in a common deterministic work unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(\varepsilon)\le N(\varepsilon)(C_{\mathrm{grad}}+C_{\mathrm{proj}}+C_{\mathrm{aux}})\).

notation.meaning: iterations required for the chosen accuracy criterion

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Vector Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box access model for a quadratic objective whose Hessian is available only through products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), matrix-vector access consists of an oracle \(\mathcal O_Q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(\mathcal O_Q(v)=Qv\). An algorithm may choose each query vector from previously returned products and its initial data, but it neither reads nor factors \(Q\). Given explicit access to \(c\), one query at \(x\) returns enough information to form \(\nabla f(x)=\mathcal O_Q(x)+c\). Oracle complexity is the number of calls to \(\mathcal O_Q\); arithmetic and storage costs are reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver may multiply chosen vectors by the quadratic matrix but may not inspect or factor that matrix; one product gives a gradient when the linear term is known.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) are fixed throughout the run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=\mathcal O_Q(x)+c\) requires one matrix-vector oracle call.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Matrix-Vector Access, and the gradient identity is correct for the displayed quadratic. The restrictions on inspecting and factoring Q are conventions defining a particular black-box model and require an authoritative, specifically located source.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Minimization Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-gradient access to a convex feasible region without Euclidean projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact. A linear-minimization oracle is a map \(\mathcal O_C:\mathbb R^n\to C\) satisfying \[\mathcal O_C(g)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle.\] Linear-minimization access permits an algorithm to submit adaptively chosen directions \(g\) and receive an arbitrary minimizing point when the minimizer is nonunique. The oracle need not return a Euclidean projection or a description of \(C\). Complexity counts calls to \(\mathcal O_C\), with gradient evaluations and arithmetic charged separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A query supplies a direction and returns a feasible point minimizing the associated linear function; no projection or explicit representation of the feasible set is required.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and compact, ensuring every query attains a minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_C(g)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle\) for every \(g\in\mathbb R^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Linear-Minimization Access, and compactness ensures attainment. However, the scope and notation call C convex while the formal statement and assumptions require only compactness. An inspectable source is also needed to establish the intended conditional-gradient oracle convention and settle whether convexity belongs among the formal hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Reusable-Factorization Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work model separating a one-time matrix factorization from repeated triangular solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let repeated algorithmic subproblems have the form \(Mz_j=r_j\), where the nonsingular matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is fixed and only \(r_j\) changes. Reusable-factorization access computes once a factorization \(M=LU\), or \(M=R^{\mathsf T}R\) when appropriate, and answers each subsequent query by triangular solves. For \(N\) right-hand sides, the work and storage model is \[W_N=C_{\mathrm{fact}}(M)+N C_{\mathrm{solve}}(M),\qquad S_N=S_{\mathrm{fact}}(M),\] rather than charging a new factorization for every query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed system matrix is factored once, after which changing right-hand sides are handled by cheaper triangular solves; total cost separates setup from per-query work.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is fixed and nonsingular across all queries.
The selected factorization is numerically admissible for \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_N=C_{\mathrm{fact}}(M)+N C_{\mathrm{solve}}(M)\).

notation.meaning: cost of one solve using stored factors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is a plausible role for this access model, and the setup-plus-solve work decomposition matches the title. The exact storage equality omits possible right-hand-side and workspace storage, while the admissible LU or Cholesky cases and accounting convention have no cited support. A numerical-linear-algebra source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convexity Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-rate mechanism for projected gradient on a strongly convex smooth quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) be \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), with \(0<\mu\le L\). For projected-gradient iterates \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k))\) and the unique minimizer \(x_*\), strong convexity converts the descent estimate into the geometric bound \[f(x_k)-f(x_*)\le\left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f(x_*)\bigr).\] Consequently, objective accuracy \(f(x_k)-f(x_*)\le\varepsilon\) requires order \((L/\mu)\log((f(x_0)-f(x_*))/\varepsilon)\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive curvature converts projected-gradient descent into geometric objective convergence, governed by the condition ratio between smoothness and strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes the intended strong-convexity rate mechanism, though property is less exact than a theorem or complexity-bound role for the displayed guarantee. The exact projected-gradient objective contraction requires a source fixing the definitions of smoothness and strong convexity on C and verifying that the stated step and factor apply under those constrained-domain hypotheses.

children.title: Quadratic-Growth Rate Mechanism
children.top_down_role: Rate regimes supported by objective growth away from the solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Rate Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restarted acceleration under quadratic growth, without requiring global strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be convex with solution set \(X_*\), and suppose \(F(x)-F_*\ge\tfrac\mu2\operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)^2\) throughout the relevant level set. Assume an accelerated first-order routine started at \(z\) satisfies \(F(x_m)-F_*\le A L\operatorname{dist}(z,X_*)^2/(m+1)^2\). Restarting after any \(m\) with \((m+1)^2\ge4AL/\mu\) halves the objective gap at every stage. Thus \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((F(x_0)-F_*)/\varepsilon))\) first-order iterations suffice for objective gap at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth lets periodic restarts turn an accelerated inverse-square rate into geometric convergence, with square-root dependence on the growth condition ratio.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex with nonempty \(X_*\).
Quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu>0\) holds on the iterates' level set.
The base routine has the displayed accelerated bound with constants \(A,L>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)=O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((F(x_0)-F_*)/\varepsilon))\).

notation.meaning: set of minimizers of the objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound fits the terminal container, and the algebraic restart mechanism is plausible from the two displayed inequalities. The base accelerated routine, relevant level-set invariance, stage initialization, and constant needed for the claimed halving schedule are not tied to any inspectable source.

children.title: Error-Bound Rate Mechanism
children.top_down_role: Rate regimes supported by residual-to-solution-set control.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Rate Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract residual error bound converting sufficient decrease into a linear objective rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an iteration map \(T\) have residual \(R(x)=x-Tx\) and preserve a region containing the solution set. Suppose constants \(a,b>0\) satisfy \[F(Tx)\le F(x)-a\|R(x)\|^2,\qquad F(x)-F_*\le b\|R(x)\|^2\] for every iterate. Then \[F(Tx)-F_*\le\left(1-\frac{a}{b}\right)(F(x)-F_*),\] provided \(a\le b\). Hence the residual domination supplied by an error bound upgrades sufficient decrease to geometric convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the step residual controls objective error and each step decreases the objective proportionally to the squared residual, objective gaps contract geometrically.
assumptions_latex: \(F_*\) is finite and the iteration remains in the region where both displayed inequalities hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication from the two displayed inequalities to a geometric objective contraction is algebraically consistent, and property is a reasonable mechanism-level role. The record provides no authoritative source for this residual error-bound framework, and the invariant region on which the inequalities hold is not defined precisely enough to validate repeated application.

children.title: Growth–Error-Bound Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Error-Bound Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convex correspondence between quadratic growth and subdifferential metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, with minimizer set \(X_*\ne\varnothing\). Near \(X_*\), the quadratic-growth property \[F(x)-F_*\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)^2\] is equivalent, up to a change of positive constants and possibly a smaller neighborhood, to the subdifferential error bound \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x)).\] Thus either condition can supply the local regularity needed for linear-rate analysis of compatible first-order residual methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex objective, local quadratic growth and a local subgradient error bound describe the same regularity, up to constants and neighborhood size.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(X_*\) is nonempty, and both predicates are interpreted locally around \(X_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{quadratic growth near }X_*\Longleftrightarrow\text{metric subregularity of }\partial F\text{ at }(X_*,0)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal container calls for a correspondence, but duality is not the precise mathematical role; theorem or property would be more appropriate. Moreover, metric subregularity is normally stated at a specified graph point, whereas “at (X_*,0)” conflates a set of points with one graph point. A source is required to fix the local or uniform version, constants, neighborhoods, and content kind before a reliable replacement can be made.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sharpness Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual sharpness converts KKT residual reduction into distance-to-solution convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex quadratic program, let \(Z_*\) be the primal-dual KKT solution set and let \(R_{\mathrm{KKT}}(z)\) collect stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity residuals. Suppose a neighborhood \(U\) of \(Z_*\) admits the sharp error bound \[\operatorname{dist}(z,Z_*)\le\kappa\|R_{\mathrm{KKT}}(z)\|.\] If an algorithm eventually remains in \(U\) and contracts this residual as \(\|R_{\mathrm{KKT}}(z_{k+1})\|\le\rho\|R_{\mathrm{KKT}}(z_k)\|\) for \(0<\rho<1\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(z_k,Z_*)\le\kappa\rho^{k-k_0}\|R_{\mathrm{KKT}}(z_{k_0})\|\) for every \(k\ge k_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local KKT error bound turns geometric contraction of a computable optimality residual into geometric convergence of primal-dual iterates to the solution set.
assumptions_latex: The convex quadratic program has a nonempty primal-dual KKT solution set.
The displayed KKT error bound holds on a neighborhood containing all iterates after index \(k_0\).
The algorithm contracts the selected KKT residual with factor \(\rho\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(z_k,Z_*)\le\kappa\rho^{k-k_0}\|R_{\mathrm{KKT}}(z_{k_0})\|\) for \(k\ge k_0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is plausible for the KKT sharpness mechanism, and the final distance estimate follows if the assumed error bound and residual contraction hold. But “collect” does not define a single KKT residual mapping, especially for complementarity and inequality violations, so the norm and error-bound claim depend materially on a missing authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Structure Identification Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite active-face identification by projected gradient under strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing a continuously differentiable convex function \(f\) over a polyhedron \(C\). Let projected-gradient iterates satisfy \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k))\), where \(x_k\to x_*\) and \(0<\underline\alpha\le\alpha_k\le\overline\alpha\). If \(-\nabla f(x_*)\) lies in the relative interior of the normal cone \(N_C(x_*)\), then there exists \(K<\infty\) such that, for every \(k\ge K\), \(x_k\) lies in the minimal face of \(C\) containing \(x_*\). Subsequent iterations therefore evolve on the identified face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convergence and strict complementarity, projected gradient reaches the solution’s minimal polyhedral face after finitely many iterations and thereafter preserves that active structure.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron and \(f\) is continuously differentiable and convex.
The projected-gradient sequence converges to \(x_*\), with step sizes bounded above and away from zero.
\(-\nabla f(x_*)\in\operatorname{ri}N_C(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists K\;\forall k\ge K:\ x_k\in\operatorname{face}_C(x_*)\).

notation.meaning: normal cone to the feasible polyhedron at the limit
minimal face of the feasible set containing the limit
Euclidean projection onto the feasible set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits this finite-identification claim. Its exact hypotheses are source-sensitive: finite minimal-face identification and subsequent preservation can depend on the projection geometry, nondegeneracy formulation, step behavior, and convergence assumptions. No source or theorem locator is supplied to validate this version.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Primal Rate Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical accelerated objective rates for smooth convex and strongly convex primal problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a closed convex set \(C\), and let accelerated projected gradient start from \(x_0\). For some minimizer \(x_*\), its convex rate satisfies \[f(x_k)-f(x_*)\le\frac{2L\|x_0-x_*\|^2}{(k+1)^2},\] giving \(O(\sqrt{L\|x_0-x_*\|^2/\varepsilon})\) gradient-projection calls. If \(f\) is additionally \(\mu\)-strongly convex, a strongly convex accelerated schedule or suitable restart attains \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(x_0)-f(x_*))/\varepsilon))\) calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration gives an inverse-square objective rate for smooth convex primal problems and square-root condition-number dependence with logarithmic accuracy under strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(C\).
For the linear-rate case, \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{cvx}}(\varepsilon)=O(\sqrt{L\|x_0-x_*\|^2/\varepsilon})\) and \(N_{\mathrm{sc}}(\varepsilon)=O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound fits the rate-family container, but the record combines a specific constant for an unnamed convex accelerated projected-gradient method with asymptotic strongly convex and restarted variants. The exact algorithm, initialization convention, constrained smoothness assumptions, and restart guarantee require a specifically located authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Primal-Dual Rate Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate hierarchy for proximal first-order methods on convex-concave bilinear saddle problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x\max_y\Phi(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h^*(y)\), with proximal access to \(g\) and \(h^*\). Under ordinary convexity and bounded comparison sets, primal-dual splitting with compatible step sizes achieves an ergodic restricted saddle gap of order \(O(1/k)\). Accelerated parameter schedules improve the appropriate restricted gap or weighted primal-dual error to \(O(1/k^2)\) when one side has a positive strong-convexity modulus. When both sides are strongly convex, suitable accelerated primal-dual schemes attain geometric error decay, with the contraction depending on the two moduli and \(\|K\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-dual splitting has an inverse-linear baseline rate; one-sided strong convexity enables inverse-square acceleration, while two-sided strong convexity can produce geometric convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h^*\) are proper, closed, and convex, and a saddle point exists.
The proximal maps of \(g\) and \(h^*\) are available and step sizes satisfy the method's coupling condition.
Accelerated cases use the stated one-sided or two-sided strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G_k=O(k^{-1})\), improving to \(O(k^{-2})\) under one-sided strong convexity and to \(O(\rho^k)\) under suitable two-sided strong convexity, where \(0<\rho<1\).

notation.meaning: method-appropriate restricted primal-dual gap or error

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is suitable for the terminal container, but the statement blends several primal-dual algorithms, gap measures, averaging rules, and strong-convexity regimes. The placeholder “method-appropriate restricted gap or error” is not one defined quantity, so the three rates cannot be reviewed as a single precise claim without algorithm-specific sources and locators.

children.title: Adaptive Restart Triggers
children.top_down_role: Observable criteria used to choose restart timing without fixed problem constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Restart Triggers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable restart conditions for accelerated projected-gradient iterations on convex quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\) be the accepted iterate and \(y_k\) the extrapolated point of an accelerated projected-gradient method. A function trigger fires when \(f(x_{k+1})>f(x_k)\); a directional trigger fires when \(\langle y_k-x_{k+1},x_{k+1}-x_k\rangle>0\). With \(\tau_k\) equal to the disjunction of these tests, an adaptive restart sets the momentum parameter to its initial value and replaces the next extrapolated point by \(y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}\) whenever \(\tau_k=1\). Otherwise the ordinary acceleration update is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restart acceleration after objective increase or adverse alignment between the gradient step and momentum displacement; reset the extrapolated point to the accepted iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(Q\succeq0\).
\(x_k,y_k\) are generated by a fixed accelerated projected-gradient scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_k=1\Longrightarrow y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}\) and the momentum state is reset.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the Adaptive Restart Triggers leaf, and the notation is delimited and internally coherent. However, no citation supports the particular objective-increase and directional tests, their sign convention, or their application to projected-gradient iterates. An authoritative restart reference with a theorem, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Sharpness-Based Restart Schedules
children.top_down_role: Restart-complexity regimes informed by growth or sharpness information.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness-Based Restart Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-period acceleration restarts derived from quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume an accelerated inner method satisfies \(f(\mathcal A_T(z))-f^*\le 2L\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)^2/(T+1)^2\). Given \(L>0\), sharpness constant \(\mu>0\), initial point \(z_0\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(T=\max\{1,\lceil\sqrt{8L/\mu}\rceil-1\}\). For \(j=0,1,\ldots\), compute \(z_{j+1}=\mathcal A_T(z_j)\), restarting the momentum state at every block boundary. Stop at the first theoretical index with \(f(z_j)-f^*\le\varepsilon\). Each block contracts the objective gap by at most one half, so the total inner-iteration count is \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(z_0)-f^*)/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run acceleration in blocks whose length is proportional to the square root of the smoothness-to-sharpness ratio, resetting momentum after each block.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\ge\tfrac\mu2\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\) for every feasible \(x\).
\(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on the feasible set.
\(0<\varepsilon<f(z_0)-f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(z_j)-f^*\le2^{-j}(f(z_0)-f^*)\) and \(N_\varepsilon=O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(z_0)-f^*)/\varepsilon))\).

notation.meaning: T-step accelerated inner method with fresh momentum

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the restart-schedule leaf, and the stated period yields the claimed one-half contraction from the displayed assumptions. No source is supplied for the accelerated inner bound, quadratic-growth restart construction, constants, or complexity conclusion, so the mathematical variant cannot be accepted without an exact locator.

children.title: Miscalibrated Restart Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity degradation caused by premature, delayed, or unstable restart decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Miscalibrated Restart Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of choosing a restart period inconsistent with quadratic sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the accelerated bound and quadratic-growth condition, a restart block of length \(T\) has certified contraction factor \(\rho_T=4L/(\mu(T+1)^2)\). If \(T+1\le2\sqrt{L/\mu}\), this estimate gives \(\rho_T\ge1\) and therefore certifies no contraction. If \(T\gg\sqrt{L/\mu}\), contraction remains possible, but each restart expends asymptotically more inner iterations than the constant-factor contraction requires. Thus periods below the condition-number scale are under-tuned, while periods far above it are over-tuned; the work-optimal scale, up to constants, is \(T=\Theta(\sqrt{L/\mu})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting too frequently destroys the available contraction guarantee; restarting much too late preserves convergence but wastes iterations. The correct scale is the square root condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(f(\mathcal A_T(z))-f^*\le2L\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)^2/(T+1)^2\).
\(f(z)-f^*\ge\tfrac\mu2\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_T=4L/(\mu(T+1)^2)\), with useful constant-factor restart periods satisfying \(T=\Theta(\sqrt{L/\mu})\).

notation.meaning: certified objective-gap factor per restart block

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role fits the Miscalibrated Restart Regimes leaf. The displayed factor follows formally from the two assumptions, but the claims that long blocks waste iterations and that the stated scale is work-optimal require a specified work criterion and authoritative source support.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal First-Order Lower-Bound Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic linear-span oracle lower bounds for smooth convex quadratic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(k\ge1\) and sufficiently large dimension, any deterministic first-order method whose iterates lie in the span of previously returned gradients admits a convex quadratic instance with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(\|x_0-x^*\|\le R\) such that \(f(x_k)-f^*\ge cLR^2/(k+1)^2\). If the instance is additionally \(\mu\)-strongly convex, there is an instance satisfying \(f(x_k)-f^*\ge c q^{2k}(f(x_0)-f^*)\), where \(q=(\sqrt{L/\mu}-1)/(\sqrt{L/\mu}+1)\) and \(c>0\) is universal. Consequently the respective worst-case iteration requirements are \(\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) and \(\Omega(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))\), with relative accuracy in the latter bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex quadratics require inverse-square-root accuracy iterations, while strongly convex quadratics require square-root-condition-number times logarithmic-accuracy iterations.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\) at queried primal points.
The method is deterministic and satisfies the linear-span restriction.
The dimension may grow with the iteration horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon=\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) in the convex case and \(N_\varepsilon=\Omega(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) in the strongly convex case.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is appropriate for this lower-bound-family topic. The claim combines convex and strongly convex oracle lower bounds whose constants, dimension requirements, oracle model, linear-span scope, and relative-accuracy normalization must be tied to exact theorem locators. No source reference is present.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Lower-Bound Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic primal-dual oracle lower bounds for bilinear saddle instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the saddle family \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\langle Ax,y\rangle\), where \(X\) and \(Y\) are Euclidean balls of radii \(R_x\) and \(R_y\). For every \(k\ge1\) and sufficiently large dimensions, any deterministic primal-dual linear-span method using the oracle \((A^{\mathsf T}y,-Ax)\) has an instance for which the ergodic or pointwise primal-dual gap after \(k\) calls is at least \(c\|A\|R_xR_y/(k+1)\), for a universal \(c>0\). Hence obtaining gap at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(\|A\|R_xR_y/\varepsilon)\) primal-dual oracle calls in this family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bilinear saddle instances force first-order primal-dual methods to use order inverse-accuracy oracle calls, scaled by coupling strength and domain radii.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and obeys a primal-dual linear-span restriction.
The dimensions may grow with \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon=\Omega(\|A\|R_xR_y/\varepsilon)\) for the bilinear primal-dual gap criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound fits the primal-dual lower-bound topic, but the phrase "ergodic or pointwise" blends distinct output and gap guarantees. An exact lower-bound theorem is needed to determine which output convention, span restriction, dimensions, and primal-dual gap definition are supported.

children.title: Iteration Counts
children.top_down_role: Cross-method iteration requirements at matched termination accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of convergence estimates into stopping-accuracy iteration counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_k\ge0\) be the prescribed error measure and define \(N_\varepsilon=\min\{k\ge0:E_k\le\varepsilon\}\). If \(E_k\le C/(k+1)^p\) with \(C>0\) and \(p>0\), then \(N_\varepsilon\le\max\{0,\lceil(C/\varepsilon)^{1/p}\rceil-1\}\). If instead \(E_k\le C\rho^k\) with \(0<\rho<1\), then \(N_\varepsilon\le\left\lceil\log(C/\varepsilon)/\log(1/\rho)\right\rceil\) whenever \(0<\varepsilon<C\). The count includes every iteration whose kernel is executed before the first certified acceptable iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration count is the first index meeting the error tolerance; polynomial and geometric convergence bounds invert into root and logarithmic counts, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \(E_k\) is the error quantity used by the stopping specification.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon\) is bounded by inversion of the available upper bound on \(E_k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound role fits Iteration Counts, and the algebraic inversions are standard and correctly delimited. Nevertheless, the record supplies no inspectable citation for the stopping-index and executed-kernel counting convention required by this knowledge layer.

children.title: Per-Iteration Linear-Algebra Cost
children.top_down_role: Kernel work incurred by each outer solver iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Per-Iteration Linear-Algebra Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse-arithmetic kernel cost for matrix-free first-order QP iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a QP with \(n\) primal variables, \(m\) linear constraints, Hessian \(Q\), and constraint matrix \(A\), suppose one iteration performs \(r_Q\) products with \(Q\), \(r_A\) products with \(A\), \(r_{A^{\mathsf T}}\) products with \(A^{\mathsf T}\), and a constant number of vector operations. In the sparse arithmetic model its cost is \(K_k=\Theta(r_Q\operatorname{nnz}(Q)+(r_A+r_{A^{\mathsf T}})\operatorname{nnz}(A)+n+m)+P_k\), where \(P_k\) is the cost of projections, proximal maps, or other non-matrix kernels. The expression excludes reusable setup and factorization work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-iteration work equals sparse matrix-vector products, vector operations, and projection or proximal costs, while reusable preprocessing is accounted for separately.
assumptions_latex: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication costs one arithmetic operation per stored entry up to constants.
The product counts are bounded independently of \(n\) and \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_k=\Theta(r_Q\operatorname{nnz}(Q)+(r_A+r_{A^{\mathsf T}})\operatorname{nnz}(A)+n+m)+P_k\).

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros of matrix M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound role fits the per-iteration cost leaf. No source supports the sparse arithmetic model, and the stated Theta expression requires explicit assumptions about matrix storage, product implementations, and whether the listed vector operations necessarily incur matching lower as well as upper costs.

children.title: Aggregate Kernel Work
children.top_down_role: Total linear-algebra effort after combining iteration count with kernel cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Kernel Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total iterative arithmetic work accumulated to the stopping iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If iteration \(k\) incurs kernel cost \(K_k\) and the stopping count is \(N_\varepsilon\), define aggregate kernel work by \(W_{\mathrm{ker}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{k=0}^{N_\varepsilon-1}K_k\). When \(K_k\le\overline K\) uniformly, \(W_{\mathrm{ker}}(\varepsilon)\le N_\varepsilon\overline K\); when \(K_k=K\) is constant, equality gives \(W_{\mathrm{ker}}(\varepsilon)=N_\varepsilon K\). This accounting includes all unsuccessful or restart-triggering iterations actually executed, but excludes one-time setup work unless that work is repeated inside the iterative kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate kernel work is the sum of all executed iteration costs through termination, including discarded or restart-triggering steps but excluding genuinely one-time setup.
assumptions_latex: \(N_\varepsilon<\infty\).
\(K_k\ge0\) measures work under a fixed computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{\mathrm{ker}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{k=0}^{N_\varepsilon-1}K_k\le N_\varepsilon\overline K\) when \(K_k\le\overline K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound role fits Aggregate Kernel Work, and the summation and uniform-cost bound are mathematically coherent. An inspectable source is still required for the accounting convention, particularly the inclusion of rejected or restart-triggering executions and exclusion of setup work.

children.title: One-Time Setup Work
children.top_down_role: Preprocessing, analysis, compilation, and factorization costs paid before solves.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Time Setup Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work decomposition separating reusable preprocessing from iterative solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) denote computation performed once for a fixed QP structure, including scaling, permutation, symbolic analysis, preconditioner construction, or factorization, and let \(W_i\) be the kernel work of solve \(i\). For \(M\) solves that reuse every setup artifact without rebuilding it, total work is represented by \(W_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)=S+\sum_{i=1}^{M}W_i\). Any update that invalidates an artifact must instead be charged as a new setup event; thus a cost is one-time only relative to the explicitly fixed data shared by the solve sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total work separates reusable preprocessing from solve-specific iterations; preprocessing is one-time only while all data on which it depends remain fixed.
assumptions_latex: The \(M\) instances share every matrix structure and numerical datum required by the reused setup artifacts.
All work is measured in one consistent cost model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)=S+\sum_{i=1}^{M}W_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits One-Time Setup Work, and the decomposition is internally consistent. No citation establishes the setup-versus-kernel accounting model or the listed classes of reusable artifacts, so an authoritative solver or computational-cost reference with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Repeated-Solve Amortization
children.top_down_role: Allocation of reusable setup costs across related QP instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Solve Amortization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-solve work after amortizing reusable setup across a QP sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\ge1\) solves sharing one setup of cost \(S\), with solve-specific kernel costs \(W_1,\ldots,W_M\), the amortized work per solve is \(\overline W_M=(S+\sum_{i=1}^{M}W_i)/M=S/M+(1/M)\sum_{i=1}^{M}W_i\). If \(W_i\le W\) uniformly, then \(\overline W_M\le S/M+W\). Consequently the setup contribution decreases exactly as \(S/M\), and \(\overline W_M\to W_\infty\) whenever the average kernel work converges to \(W_\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide reusable setup work across all solves: its per-solve contribution is setup cost divided by sequence length, plus average iterative work.
assumptions_latex: The setup artifact is valid and reused for all \(M\) solves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline W_M=S/M+(1/M)\sum_{i=1}^{M}W_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits Repeated-Solve Amortization, and the formula and limiting statement are correct under the stated assumptions. The candidate has no inspectable source for this computational accounting model.

children.title: Break-Even Solve Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solve-count regimes where reusable preparation offsets its initial cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Break-Even Solve Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solve-count threshold for preferring a setup-intensive solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compare solvers \(A\) and \(B\) over \(M\) repeated instances, with setup costs \(S_A,S_B\) and constant per-solve kernel costs \(K_A,K_B\). Solver \(A\) has no greater total work precisely when \(S_A+MK_A\le S_B+MK_B\). If \(S_A>S_B\) and \(K_A<K_B\), the smallest break-even count is \(M_{\mathrm{be}}=\left\lceil(S_A-S_B)/(K_B-K_A)\right\rceil\), and \(A\) is preferable for every integer \(M\ge M_{\mathrm{be}}\). If \(K_A\ge K_B\) while \(S_A>S_B\), no finite break-even count exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A setup-intensive solver becomes cheaper once accumulated per-solve savings cover its extra setup cost; otherwise no finite break-even point exists.
assumptions_latex: \(S_A,S_B,K_A,K_B\ge0\).
Per-solve costs are constant over the compared sequence.
Both solvers meet the same accuracy requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_A+MK_A\le S_B+MK_B\), with \(M_{\mathrm{be}}=\lceil(S_A-S_B)/(K_B-K_A)\rceil\) when \(S_A>S_B\) and \(K_A<K_B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits Break-Even Solve Regimes, and the threshold formula is coherent for integer solve counts under constant costs. No source supports the model or its applicability to repeated QP solves; a precise cost-model locator is required.

children.title: Communication Complexity
children.top_down_role: Synchronization, message-count, and data-movement costs across solver architectures.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed communication counts and latency-bandwidth time for first-order QP iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a distributed first-order QP iteration performs at most \(r\) communication rounds and transfers at most \(b\) words on the critical path. After \(N_\varepsilon\) iterations, excluding setup, the communication complexity is at most \(R_\varepsilon=rN_\varepsilon\) rounds and \(B_\varepsilon=bN_\varepsilon\) words. In the latency-bandwidth model with latency \(\alpha\) per round and inverse bandwidth \(\beta\) per word, communication time satisfies \(T_{\mathrm{comm}}\le N_\varepsilon(\alpha r+\beta b)\). Setup communication \((R_0,B_0)\) is included by replacing these totals with \((R_0+R_\varepsilon,B_0+B_\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply per-iteration synchronization rounds and transferred words by the iteration count, then add setup communication; latency and bandwidth weight the two totals separately.
assumptions_latex: The same distributed data layout is used throughout the solve.
\(r\) and \(b\) uniformly bound critical-path communication per iteration.
Communication and computation are not overlapped in the stated time bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathrm{tot}}\le R_0+rN_\varepsilon\), \(B_{\mathrm{tot}}\le B_0+bN_\varepsilon\), and \(T_{\mathrm{comm}}\le\alpha R_{\mathrm{tot}}+\beta B_{\mathrm{tot}}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound role fits Communication Complexity. The round and word totals are coherent under uniform per-iteration bounds, but no source supports the latency-bandwidth model or its critical-path interpretation. The relationship between the no-overlap assumption and the asserted communication-time upper bound also needs source-specific clarification.

children.title: Memory Footprint
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements for problem data, iterates, factors, and workspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Footprint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage bound for sparse, matrix-free first-order QP implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a QP with primal dimension \(n\), constraint dimension \(m\), Hessian \(P\), and constraint matrix \(A\). An implementation storing both sparse matrices, a constant number of primal-dual work vectors, and \(q\) auxiliary history vectors requires
\[M=O\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(P)+\operatorname{nnz}(A)+n+m+q(n+m)\right)\]
scalar words. If matrix-vector products with \(P\) and \(A\) are supplied by oracles, explicit matrix storage disappears and the bound becomes \(M=O((q+1)(n+m))\), excluding oracle-internal storage and preprocessing data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse storage scales with matrix nonzeros plus primal-dual work vectors; matrix-free implementations retain only vectors, apart from storage hidden inside multiplication oracles.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) are stored sparsely or accessed through multiplication oracles.
The algorithm uses a constant number of current iterates and residual vectors plus \(q\) history vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[M=O\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(P)+\operatorname{nnz}(A)+(q+1)(n+m)\right).\]

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros of matrix B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The storage estimate is plausible, but no inspectable source is supplied and the dimensions of the q history vectors are not stated, so the q(n+m) term is not justified as written.

children.title: Bandwidth-Limited Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solver behavior when data movement dominates arithmetic work.

knowledge_statements.title: Bandwidth-Limited Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Roofline condition for bandwidth domination of a QP iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let one solver iteration perform \(F\) floating-point operations and transfer \(B>0\) bytes between the limiting memory level and the processor. With peak arithmetic throughput \(\pi\) and sustainable bandwidth \(\beta\), its arithmetic intensity is \(I=F/B\). Under the roofline cost model, the iteration is bandwidth-limited precisely when
\[\frac{F}{\pi}<\frac{B}{\beta},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad I<\frac{\pi}{\beta}.\]
In this regime the predicted iteration time is \(T\ge B/\beta\), so reducing arithmetic without reducing transferred bytes does not improve the modelled bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iteration is bandwidth-limited when its arithmetic intensity lies below the machine balance; runtime is then bounded by bytes transferred divided by sustainable bandwidth.
assumptions_latex: Computation and data movement obey the roofline lower-bound model \(T\ge\max\{F/\pi,B/\beta\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[I<\pi/\beta\ \Longrightarrow\ T\ge B/\beta.\]

notation.meaning: arithmetic intensity in operations per byte

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is standard under a roofline model, but the record supplies no source for the model or the claimed bandwidth-limited interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Definite KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric quasi-definite saddle-point matrices arising in regularized splitting steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A symmetric block matrix
\[K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&-D\end{bmatrix}\]
is quasi-definite when \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}\) and \(D\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}\), with arbitrary \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). Such \(K\) is nonsingular and has inertia \((n,m,0)\). In particular, if \(P\succeq0\), then the regularized KKT matrix with \(H=P+\rho I\), \(D=\delta I\), and \(\rho,\delta>0\) is quasi-definite, independently of the rank of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-definite primal and negative-definite dual diagonal blocks make a symmetric KKT matrix quasi-definite, nonsingular, and of fixed inertia.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}\), \(D\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}\), and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\text{ is nonsingular and }\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0).\]

notation.meaning: numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and inertia claim are mathematically standard and fit the container, but the nontrivial nonsingularity and fixed-inertia assertions have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Equation Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite normal equations for a regularized weighted least-squares subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}\), \(P\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\). Consider
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \frac12(Ax-b)^{\mathsf T}W(Ax-b)+\frac12(x-c)^{\mathsf T}P(x-c).\]
Its first-order equation is
\[(P+A^{\mathsf T}WA)x=Pc+A^{\mathsf T}Wb.\]
The coefficient matrix is positive definite exactly when \(\ker(P)\cap\ker(A)=\{0\}\); under this condition the normal equation has a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted quadratic problem has a primal normal equation whose coefficient matrix is positive definite exactly when the Hessian and constraint terms have no common null direction.
assumptions_latex: \(W\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}\), \(P\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n}\), and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
\(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and \(\ker(P)\cap\ker(A)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(P+A^{\mathsf T}WA)x=Pc+A^{\mathsf T}Wb\quad\text{has a unique solution}.\]

notation.meaning: weighted quadratic form induced by W

knowledge_statements.title: Schur-Complement Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual Schur-complement reduction of a regularized KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}\), \(D\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{m}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(r\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and \(s\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\). Consider
\[\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&-D\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r\\s\end{bmatrix}.\]
Eliminating \(x=H^{-1}(r-A^{\mathsf T}y)\) gives
\[(D+AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})y=AH^{-1}r-s.\]
The Schur complement is positive definite exactly when \(\ker(D)\cap\ker(A^{\mathsf T})=\{0\}\). Under this condition, solving the Schur system and recovering \(x\) gives the unique solution of the original system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the primal block produces a dual Schur system. It is positive definite when the dual regularizer and transposed constraint matrix have no common null direction.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{n}\), \(D\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{m}\), and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
\(r\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(s\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), and \(\ker(D)\cap\ker(A^{\mathsf T})=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(D+AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})y=AH^{-1}r-s,\qquad x=H^{-1}(r-A^{\mathsf T}y).\]

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Reduced Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Null-space reduction of an equality-constrained convex quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), where \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\) and \(Ax=b\) is consistent. Consider
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \frac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+q^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b.\]
Let \(x_p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\) satisfy \(Ax_p=b\), and let the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) form a basis of \(\ker(A)\). Every feasible point is \(x=x_p+Zp\), with \(p\in\mathbb{R}^{n-m}\), and stationarity reduces to
\[(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)p=-Z^{\mathsf T}(Hx_p+q).\]
If \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\succ0\), this system has a unique solution and yields the unique constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameterizing feasible points by a null-space basis converts the equality-constrained QP into a reduced system. Positive definiteness of the reduced Hessian gives a unique constrained minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\).
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\) and \(Ax=b\) is consistent.
\(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p=-(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)^{-1}Z^{\mathsf T}(Hx_p+q),\qquad x^\star=x_p+Zp.\]

notation.meaning: full-column-rank basis matrix for the null space of A

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Symmetric Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-based direct solution of sparse symmetric QP systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a sparse nonsingular symmetric matrix \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{N}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{N}\), choose a symmetric permutation \(\Pi\) and compute a possibly pivoted factorization
\[\Pi K\Pi^{\mathsf T}=LDL^{\mathsf T},\]
where \(L\) is unit lower triangular and \(D\) is block diagonal with nonsingular \(1\times1\) and, when required, \(2\times2\) pivot blocks. Solve \(Lz=\Pi b\), \(Dw=z\), and \(L^{\mathsf T}u=w\), then return \(x=\Pi^{\mathsf T}u\). The ordering and pivoting strategy seek to control fill while meeting the implementation's numerical-stability criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse symmetric system is permuted, factored into triangular and block-diagonal factors, and solved by two triangular substitutions and a block-diagonal solve.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb{S}^{N}\) is sparse and nonsingular, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{N}\).
The pivoting rule selects nonsingular diagonal blocks and terminates without numerical breakdown.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Kx=b,\qquad x=\Pi^{\mathsf T}L^{-\mathsf T}D^{-1}L^{-1}\Pi b.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Fill-Reducing Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural ordering objective for sparse symmetric factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a symmetric sparsity pattern \(G\) and an elimination permutation \(\pi\), let \(L(\pi;G)\) denote the symbolic lower-triangular factor pattern produced by eliminating vertices in order \(\pi\). A fill-reducing ordering is any permutation selected to decrease
\[\operatorname{fill}(\pi;G)=\operatorname{nnz}(L(\pi;G))-N-\lvert E(G)\rvert\]
relative to a specified baseline ordering; an optimal fill ordering minimizes this quantity over all permutations. The definition is structural: it depends on the sparsity graph and elimination rule, not on the numerical values of structurally present entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fill-reducing ordering permutes a symmetric sparsity graph so symbolic elimination creates fewer new factor entries than a chosen baseline.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the undirected structural graph of an \(N\times N\) symmetric matrix.
Symbolic elimination uses a fixed rule for forming filled edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\pi_\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\pi}\operatorname{nnz}(L(\pi;G))\]

notation.meaning: symbolic factor pattern under ordering pi
